title: How Steve Jobs and Woz turned a hobby into Apple, and the 1977 New Yorker interview
summary: Jobs recalls how Apple began: two teenagers built a computer because they wanted one, then stumbled into a business when a store demanded assembled units. In the 1977 New Yorker interview, a 22-year-old Jobs frames the Apple II as a "domesticated" Rolls-Royce computer that teaches people about computing.

principles.text: Build the thing because you want it yourself; real businesses can grow out of scratching your own itch.
principles.quote: The reason we [Woz and I] built a computer was that we wanted one, and we couldn’t afford to buy one.

principles.text: Remove the friction in making a product; cutting assembly time dramatically unlocks demand.
principles.quote: we could cut the assembly time down from maybe fifty hours to more like an hour.

principles.text: Listen to what customers actually want; the market can reshape your plan with a twist you never considered.
principles.quote: “Well, I’ll take fifty of these computers, but I want them fully assembled.” Which was a twist that we’d never thought of.

principles.text: Making a product is not enough; you must learn sales and distribution to turn it into cash.
principles.quote: We decided we had to start learning about sales and distribution so that we could sell the fifty computers and get back our money.

principles.text: If established companies pass on your idea, start your own company.
principles.quote: Neither one was interested in pursuing it, so we started our own company.

principles.text: Great partnerships can rest on a shared passion even when people are otherwise very different.
principles.quote: we had a common interest [in electronics] that sort of bound us together even though we were totally different in every other way possible.
